title: Heidegger: Being and Time
subtitle: What does it mean to be, and what does it mean to live as one who will die?
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain why Heidegger thought the question of Being had been forgotten.
By the end you will be able to describe Dasein and being-in-the-world using the example of tools.
By the end you will be able to explain the they (das Man), authenticity and being-toward-death.
By the end you will be able to outline Heidegger's later critique of technology.
By the end you will be able to weigh the evidence about Heidegger's Nazism and the debate about what it means for his philosophy.
hook:
Think of the last time you used a hammer, or a keyboard, or a bicycle. While things were going well, did you notice the tool at all? Probably not. You noticed the nail, the sentence, the road. The tool disappeared into the task. Then the hammer head flew off, the key stuck, the chain slipped, and suddenly there it was: an object, sitting there, demanding attention.

This small observation sits at the heart of one of the most influential and most difficult books of the twentieth century, Martin Heidegger's *Being and Time* (1927). Heidegger thought that Western philosophy since Plato had made a basic mistake: it treated the world as a collection of objects to be looked at, when our primary relation to things is using them, caring about them, being absorbed in a world. From that starting point he built a picture of human existence that shaped existentialism, psychology, architecture and theology. And yet the man who wrote it joined the Nazi Party in 1933. Today you meet both the thinker and the problem.

sections.heading: The Forgotten Question
sections.body:
Martin Heidegger (1889–1976) was born in Messkirch, a small Catholic town in south-west Germany, the son of a church sexton. He trained first for the priesthood, then turned to philosophy. At Freiburg he became Husserl's assistant (Day 75), and Husserl saw him as his heir. Heidegger taught at Marburg from 1923, where his lectures became legendary; Hannah Arendt, whom you will meet on Day 80, said rumours spread through Germany of a hidden king of thought.

*Being and Time* opens by asking a question that sounds either trivially easy or impossible: what is the meaning of **Being**? Not what kinds of beings there are (trees, numbers, people), but what it *is* for anything to be at all. Heidegger called the difference between beings and their Being the **ontological difference**. (**Ontology** is the study of being.) He claimed philosophy had forgotten this question. Since Plato and Aristotle (Days 11 and 18), philosophers had tended to treat Being as if it were just the most general property of things, or the presence of a solid substance, or the highest being, God. They asked about beings, and let Being itself slip from view.

Where do we start? Heidegger notices that there is one being for whom its own being is an issue: us. A stone does not wonder what it is to be. We do; in fact we cannot help taking some stand on what our lives are about. So the investigation must start with an analysis of the being that asks the question. Heidegger called this being **Dasein**, an ordinary German word for existence, literally *being-there*. He chose it deliberately instead of words like *subject*, *mind*, *consciousness* or *human being*, each of which carried centuries of assumptions he wanted to avoid. Dasein is not a thing with properties; it is a way of being, an existence always already caught up in caring about something.

sections.heading: Being-in-the-World: Hammers Before Theories
sections.body:
Descartes (Day 43) began with a thinking subject inside its own mind and then worried whether an external world existed. Heidegger thought the very setup was wrong. Dasein is not a mind looking out at a world; it is **being-in-the-world**, written with hyphens to show it is a single, unified phenomenon. We are not *in* the world as water is in a glass, but as someone is *in* love or *in* business: involved, absorbed, at home. Heidegger even remarked that the scandal of philosophy is not that no one has yet proved the existence of the external world, as Kant had complained, but that such proofs keep being expected and attempted.

His famous analysis concerns equipment. In everyday life we encounter things mostly as **ready-to-hand** (*zuhanden*): hammers, doors, pens, shoes, used fluently in the flow of activity. A ready-to-hand thing is defined by what it is *for*, and it points to a whole network of other things: the hammer is for nails, nails are for boards, boards for building a shelf, the shelf for holding books, and all of it ultimately *for the sake of* some way Dasein understands itself, as a carpenter, a parent, a student. That network of significance is what Heidegger means by a **world**.

Only when something breaks down does it show up as **present-at-hand** (*vorhanden*): a mere object with properties, weight, shape, material, the kind of thing a scientist measures. Philosophers, Heidegger thinks, took this detached, staring mode as the basic way things are, when it is really a special, derivative case. Theory starts when practice is interrupted.

This idea has proved extraordinarily fertile. Hubert Dreyfus used it in the 1970s to argue that early artificial intelligence was doomed because it tried to represent the world as a vast collection of present-at-hand facts and rules, when human intelligence rests on skilled, embodied coping. Designers speak of tools that disappear in use, and good user interfaces are those you never notice.

sections.heading: Thrown Among the They
sections.body:
Dasein never starts from scratch. Heidegger says we are **thrown** (*Geworfenheit*): we find ourselves already in a particular time, place, body, language, family and history we did not choose. Our moods reveal this: we are always already in some mood, attuned to the world as threatening, boring, joyful.

And who are we, mostly? Heidegger's answer is unsettling: in everyday life, we are not really ourselves at all. We are **the they** (*das Man*, from the German impersonal pronoun, as in English *one*: *one doesn't do that*). We take pleasure as *they* take pleasure; we read, see and judge literature as *they* see and judge; we find shocking what *they* find shocking. The they is not any particular group of people. It is the anonymous, everyone-and-no-one standard of normality that tells us how one lives.

The they has its own way of talking, which Heidegger calls **idle talk** (*Gerede*): passing on what everyone says without ever touching the thing itself. Its curiosity jumps from novelty to novelty without dwelling anywhere. And it **levels down** every possibility to the average: anything original is quickly made familiar, everything great becomes common knowledge. The they also takes over responsibility; when everyone decided, no one decided.

Heidegger insists this is not a moral criticism of ordinary people; it is a structure of everyday existence that belongs to all of us. He calls our absorption in it **falling**. But it has a cost: it conceals from us that our lives are *ours*, that we could own them. The they tranquillises us, especially about the one thing it most wants to avoid talking about.

sections.heading: Anxiety, Death and Authenticity
sections.body:
That thing is death. The they certainly admits that *one dies*, eventually, someday, but not yet, and not really me. Heidegger argues this evasion hides the most important truth about Dasein. Death is my **ownmost** possibility: no one can die my death for me. It is certain, but its timing is indefinite. And it is the possibility of the end of all my possibilities.

Heidegger's term is **being-toward-death**. He does not mean brooding over dying, or thinking about the medical event, and certainly not seeking it. He means living in the awareness that my existence is finite, that my possibilities are limited and that I cannot hand off my life to anyone else. Recall the Stoic practice of remembering mortality (Day 26) and Epicurus' argument that death is nothing to us (Day 24). Heidegger is closer to the Stoics: facing finitude clarifies what matters.

This awareness often arrives through **anxiety** (*Angst*). Fear has a definite object: the dog, the exam. Anxiety has none. In anxiety, the familiar world suddenly loses its grip, everything seems to slip away, and the they's reassurances go silent. Heidegger, building on Kierkegaard (Day 64), thinks anxiety is precious: it individualises us, tearing us out of the they and confronting us with our own existence.

From this comes **authenticity** (*Eigentlichkeit*, from *eigen*, own: literally *ownedness*). To exist authentically is not to reject society or invent values from nothing; Dasein always lives among others and takes up possibilities from its shared heritage. It means to take ownership of those possibilities, to choose them in the light of finitude rather than drifting along with what *one* does. Heidegger calls this **resoluteness**. The call to it comes from **conscience**, which for him is not a moral rulebook but the silent call of Dasein to itself, summoning it back from lostness in the they.

Underlying all of this is **care** (*Sorge*): Dasein's being is care, a constant being-ahead-of-itself toward possibilities, already thrown into a world and absorbed among things. And care, Heidegger argued, is ultimately rooted in **temporality**, which is why the book is called *Being and Time*. It was never finished: the planned second half never appeared.

sections.heading: The Turn and the Question Concerning Technology
sections.body:
After the 1930s Heidegger's thinking shifted, a change he and his readers call the **turn** (*Kehre*). He wrote less about Dasein and more about the history of Being itself: the way, in each epoch, beings show up in a particular light. He wrote about poetry, especially Friedrich Hölderlin, about art, about language as the house of Being, and about dwelling.

His most influential later essay is “The Question Concerning Technology” (1954). Technology, he says, is not just a collection of machines; it is a way of revealing the world. Modern technology reveals everything as **standing-reserve** (*Bestand*): resources on call, waiting to be ordered, optimised and used. A river once revealed as a river now shows up as a supply of hydroelectric power; a forest as timber stock; human beings, eventually, as human resources. Heidegger called this framework of revealing *Gestell*, usually translated **enframing**.

He did not think we could simply switch technology off, and he was not simply anti-technology. The danger is that enframing becomes the *only* way anything can show up, so that we forget other ways of relating to the world, such as the craftsman's respect for his material or the poet's attention to things. Heidegger's late writings are often obscure and sometimes mystical, but this essay has been foundational for philosophy of technology and environmental thought (Days 88 and 89).

sections.heading: The Nazi Problem
sections.body:
Now the hard part. In April 1933, a few months after Hitler came to power, Heidegger was elected rector of the University of Freiburg. He joined the Nazi Party on 1 May 1933. His rectoral address spoke of the German university's mission in the service of the people's destiny, and in speeches to students that autumn he urged support for the Führer. He implemented the regime's restructuring of the university. He resigned the rectorship in April 1934, but remained a party member until the end of the war in 1945.

After the war, a denazification committee barred him from teaching; the ban was lifted around 1950–51. He never publicly apologised or clearly condemned the Holocaust. In a 1966 interview with *Der Spiegel*, published at his request only after his death, he defended his conduct. One notorious remark from a 1949 lecture placed the mechanised food industry and the manufacture of corpses in gas chambers side by side as expressions of the same technological essence, a comparison many readers find morally obscene.

In 2014 publication began of his private *Black Notebooks*, philosophical diaries from the 1930s and 1940s. They contain passages linking Jews, in stereotyped terms, to rootless calculation and the uprooting of the world. These ended any hope that his Nazism was a brief, opportunistic error unconnected to his thought.

How should we respond? Scholars divide. Some, like Emmanuel Faye, argue his philosophy is contaminated at the root and should not be taught as philosophy at all. Others separate the man from the work, noting that Jewish thinkers deeply influenced by him, Arendt, Herbert Marcuse, Emmanuel Levinas, Hans Jonas, took up his ideas while condemning his politics. Many worry about specific features of *Being and Time*: its talk of a people's destiny and heritage, its contempt for the they and for public opinion, its lack of an ethics of the other person. The responsible conclusion is to read Heidegger critically, never as an authority, asking at each step whether his ideas carry his politics with them.

modernConnection.title: The They in Your Pocket
modernConnection.body:
Heidegger wrote about das Man nearly a century before social media, yet his description reads uncannily like a feed. Trending topics are a literal ranking of what *they* are talking about. The phrase *everyone is saying* is now measured in shares and views. Idle talk, passing on what is said without ever engaging the thing itself, is what happens when a headline is shared by people who never read the article. Curiosity that leaps from novelty to novelty, never dwelling, describes an endlessly scrolling video app. And levelling down: every original style becomes a template, every meme is copied until it is exhausted, and recommendation systems steer each of us toward what people like us tend to like.

The analysis also helps explain why it can be so hard to notice. For Heidegger, the they is not an external authority you can rebel against; it is the default mode of being ourselves. Most of us do not feel manipulated by trends; we feel we are simply doing what one does.

His tool analysis applies too. A smartphone is ready-to-hand to an extraordinary degree: we reach for it without noticing, and it shows up as an object only when the battery dies or the screen cracks. And his later essay on technology seems to anticipate a world in which our attention, our movements and our relationships become standing-reserve, data on call to be optimised.

But be honest about the limits. Heidegger's contempt for the public sphere and for ordinary opinion fed his anti-democratic politics, and it is a poor basis for thinking about online life. Social media also connects isolated people, spreads important information, and gives voice to those excluded from older media. Authenticity cannot mean withdrawing into a heroic solitude above the crowd. A better lesson is his own: to notice when we are speaking as the they, and occasionally to ask what we ourselves think, in the light of a life that is finite and ours.

vocabulary.definition: Heidegger's distinction between beings (particular things that exist) and Being (what it is for anything to be).
vocabulary.example: Asking what kinds of animals exist is a question about beings; asking what it means for anything to exist at all respects the ontological difference.

vocabulary.definition: Heidegger's term for the kind of being humans are: a being whose own being is an issue for it and which always already understands itself in a world.
vocabulary.example: Unlike a rock, Dasein wonders what to make of its life.

vocabulary.definition: The unified structure of Dasein's existence as involved in a world of meaningful activities rather than as a mind facing external objects.
vocabulary.example: A cook absorbed in making dinner, moving among knives, pans and timers, shows being-in-the-world.

vocabulary.definition: The mode in which equipment is encountered in fluent use, defined by what it is for and largely unnoticed.
vocabulary.example: While you are typing smoothly, the keyboard is ready-to-hand.

vocabulary.definition: The anonymous, average standard of what one does, through which everyday Dasein understands itself and avoids owning its existence.
vocabulary.example: Choosing a career because it is what one does after a law degree is living by the they.

vocabulary.definition: Living in awareness of one's own finitude, that death is certain, indefinite in timing and one's ownmost possibility.
vocabulary.example: A person who reorders her priorities after realising that her time is limited is beginning to live being-toward-death.

vocabulary.definition: For Heidegger, owning one's existence: choosing one's possibilities resolutely in the light of finitude rather than drifting with the they.
vocabulary.example: Authenticity is not being different for its own sake, but making a life one's own.

vocabulary.definition: In Heidegger's later thought, the modern technological way of revealing everything as standing-reserve, resources to be ordered and used.
vocabulary.example: Seeing a mountain only as a source of minerals and a forest only as timber stock reflects enframing.

thinkingExercise.title: A Day with the They
thinkingExercise.prompt: Use Heidegger's ideas to audit one ordinary day, and then ask what owning your choices would look like.
steps: Recall yesterday. List five things you did or opinions you expressed. For each, ask: did I choose this, or is it what one does?
Find one example of idle talk: a view you repeated without having examined the thing itself.
Identify a moment when a tool broke down or got in your way. What did you notice about it that you normally do not?
Imagine you had one year left to live. Which of your five items would you keep, change or drop? Be specific.
Write a paragraph: is Heidegger's authenticity a healthy ideal or a dangerous one? Consider his own political choices in your answer.

summary: Heidegger's *Being and Time* (1927) asks the forgotten question of the meaning of Being, starting with Dasein, the being for whom its own being is an issue.
Dasein is being-in-the-world: we primarily encounter things as ready-to-hand equipment in meaningful activity, and only secondarily as present-at-hand objects.
Thrown into a world, we usually live as the they, absorbed in idle talk and average opinion; anxiety and being-toward-death can call us back to authenticity.
The later Heidegger argued that modern technology reveals everything as standing-reserve, a framework he called enframing.
Heidegger joined the Nazi Party in 1933, never publicly repented, and his *Black Notebooks* contain antisemitic passages; scholars still debate how far this taints his philosophy.

quiz.question: Why did Heidegger use the word Dasein instead of *subject* or *mind*?
options: Because it was a technical term from Aristotle
To avoid centuries of assumptions carried by those words and focus on existence as a way of being
Because he wanted to refer only to Germans
Because he denied that humans have minds
quiz.explanation: Dasein, literally being-there, was chosen to avoid the Cartesian baggage of subject and consciousness and to highlight that our being is an issue for us.

quiz.question: According to Heidegger, when does a hammer typically show up as a present-at-hand object?
options: When it is being used smoothly
When it is part of a network of equipment
When it breaks or fails
When it is ready-to-hand
quiz.explanation: In fluent use equipment is ready-to-hand and unnoticed; breakdown makes it stand out as a mere object with properties.

quiz.question: Heidegger's das Man refers to a specific social class that he believed was corrupting society.
quiz.explanation: The they is not any particular group; it is the anonymous standard of what one does, a structure of everyday existence for all of us.

quiz.question: How does Heidegger distinguish anxiety from fear?
options: Anxiety has no definite object, while fear is of something specific
Fear is always irrational, anxiety rational
Anxiety is a bodily feeling, fear a thought
They are the same thing
quiz.explanation: Following Kierkegaard, Heidegger says fear is of the dog or the exam, whereas in anxiety the world as a whole slips away.

quiz.question: Which statement best captures being-toward-death?
options: Seeking out danger to feel alive
Thinking constantly about the medical details of dying
Believing in life after death
Living with awareness that one's existence is finite and one's own
quiz.explanation: Being-toward-death is not brooding or seeking death but owning one's finite possibilities.

quiz.question: A town sees its river only as a source of hydroelectric power and its forests only as timber. Which later Heideggerian concept fits?
options: Thrownness
Enframing and standing-reserve
Idle talk
Ready-to-hand
quiz.explanation: In “The Question Concerning Technology” Heidegger argues that modern technology reveals everything as standing-reserve, resources on call.

quiz.question: Heidegger joined the Nazi Party in 1933 and remained a member until 1945.
quiz.explanation: He joined on 1 May 1933, resigned the rectorship in 1934, but kept his party membership until the end of the war.

quiz.question: Hubert Dreyfus used Heidegger's tool analysis to criticise which project?
options: Logical positivism
Early artificial intelligence based on explicit rules and facts
Marxist economics
Utilitarian ethics
quiz.explanation: Dreyfus argued that human intelligence rests on skilled coping with ready-to-hand equipment, not on representing present-at-hand facts and rules.

quiz.question: What did the publication of the *Black Notebooks* beginning in 2014 reveal?
options: That Heidegger had secretly opposed the Nazis
That Heidegger plagiarised Husserl
Passages linking Jews in stereotyped terms to rootless calculation, damaging claims that his Nazism was a brief error
The lost second half of *Being and Time*
quiz.explanation: The notebooks contain antisemitic passages woven into his philosophical reflections, intensifying the debate about his work.

quiz.question: *Being and Time* was completed as planned, with all its projected parts published in 1927.
quiz.explanation: The book was never finished; the second half, which was to address Being and time more directly, never appeared.

goDeeper.body:
Two debates are worth pursuing. The first is about **what authenticity really means**. Many early readers, including Sartre, read *Being and Time* as an existentialist manifesto about individual choice. Heidegger rejected that reading in his “Letter on Humanism” (1946), insisting his concern was always Being, not the self. Some scholars, like Charles Guignon, read authenticity as a way of taking up one's heritage with clarity and commitment, which makes it communal rather than individualistic. Critics such as Theodor Adorno, in *The Jargon of Authenticity* (1964), attacked the whole vocabulary as a pompous, empty mystique that dressed up conformity as depth. The fact that authenticity in *Being and Time* has no content, no criteria for what to choose, is exactly what worries ethicists: resoluteness could serve any cause.

The second debate is the famous **Davos encounter** of 1929, when Heidegger debated the neo-Kantian Ernst Cassirer, a liberal Jewish philosopher, at a conference in Switzerland. Cassirer defended reason, culture and the human ability to rise above finitude through symbolic forms; Heidegger insisted on human finitude and thrownness. Many witnesses, including young Emmanuel Levinas and Rudolf Carnap, felt they were watching a changing of the guard. Peter Gordon's *Continental Divide* argues the encounter became a founding myth for the split between continental and analytic philosophy, and for opposing attitudes to modernity itself.

Finally, Heidegger's influence on psychotherapy, through Medard Boss and Ludwig Binswanger's Daseinsanalysis, and on architecture, through the essay “Building Dwelling Thinking” (1951), shows how far his ideas travelled beyond philosophy.

readings.title: Being and Time
readings.author: Martin Heidegger
readings.note: Read the introduction and Division One, sections 15–16 (equipment) and 25–27 (the they). The Macquarrie and Robinson translation is standard.

readings.title: Being-in-the-World: A Commentary on Heidegger's Being and Time, Division I
readings.author: Hubert Dreyfus
readings.note: The most readable guide to the first half of the book, connected to cognitive science and AI.

readings.title: The Question Concerning Technology and Other Essays
readings.author: Martin Heidegger
readings.note: The title essay is the best entry point to the later Heidegger.

readings.title: Heidegger's Children
readings.author: Richard Wolin
readings.note: A critical study of Arendt, Löwith, Jonas and Marcuse, his Jewish students, and how they wrestled with his politics.

questions: Can a philosophy be separated from its author's politics? Does it matter which philosophy and which politics?
Is authenticity a worthwhile ideal if it gives no guidance about what to choose?
What in your own life is so ready-to-hand that you never notice it? What would it take to see it?
